title: Zone visibility (contentsHidden/contentsVisibleToOwner) is silently lost on every snapshot restore — hidden hands leak to all players
trap: The docs, Space docstring, and every example game (go-fish game.ts:56-64, cribbage game.ts:167-189) model configuring hidden information via zone visibility in the game constructor: `deck.contentsHidden(); hand.contentsVisibleToOwner()`. But `_zoneVisibility` is a `_`-prefixed private field listed in `Space.unserializableAttributes` (space.ts:114-118), so `toJSON()` never emits it — and `Game.loadSerializedState` (game.ts:2848-2857) discards the constructor-built tree (`this._t.children = []`) and rebuilds every Space via `fromJSON`, which never restores zone visibility. Proven end-to-end: after `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` (the documented 'SINGLE sanctioned way' to restore checkpoints, used by undo and server restore), `game.toJSONForPlayer(opponent)` for a `contentsVisibleToOwner()` hand went from `{"__hidden":true}` placeholders to the full card identity (`{"name":"secret","rank":"A"}`). One undo or server restart and every opponent hand and deck order is broadcast in cleartext.
rightWay: There is no right way today short of the developer knowing to re-apply zone visibility after every restore (no hook exists for this) or using only per-element `_visibility` (piece.hideFromAll()/showOnlyTo()), which IS serialized (game-element.ts:794 emits `json.visibility` when explicit). Nothing in the API or docs distinguishes the durable per-element mechanism from the volatile zone mechanism — they look equivalent and the zone one is the one the docs teach.
suggestion: Serialize `_zoneVisibility` (it's plain data — mode + player lists) in Space's toJSON/fromJSON exactly like element-level `_visibility` already is, and add a round-trip test asserting `toJSONForPlayer(opponent)` is identical before/after `GameRunner.fromSnapshot`. The SEC-02 hidden-attrs regression sweep should also run against a restored game, not only a live one.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed by direct code reading and an executable repro; I could not refute it. (1) Mechanism verified: `_zoneVisibility` is in `Space.unserializableAttributes` (src/engine/element/space.ts:114-118) so `toJSON()` never emits it; only per-element explicit `_visibility` is serialized (src/engine/element/game-element.ts:793-795). `Game.loadSerializedState` (src/engine/element/game.ts:2848+) does `this._t.children = []` and rebuilds every Space via `GameElement.fromJSON`, so the constructor-applied zone visibility is discarded and never restored. `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` (src/runtime/runner.ts:535-600) calls exactly this, and `GameSession.restore` (src/session/game-session.ts:785) and the undo/rewind checkpoint paths (stateless-ops runnerFromSnapshot/runnerFromCheckpoint) all go through it with no re-application of zone visibility. (2) Empirically reproduced: a minimal vitest game with `hand.contentsVisibleToOwner()` shows opponent `toJSONForPlayer(2)` leak = false before snapshot restore, true after `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` (test failed on the after-restore assertion). (3) The codebase itself admits the hazard: src/session/stateless-ops.ts:218-222 says the spectator view MUST be built from the LIVE runner because "zone visibility ... is NOT serialized, so a fromSnapshot reconstruction would lose it and over-reveal" — a spot workaround for one sub-path, with no guard on the general restore/undo paths. (4) It is squarely the easy path: docs, the Space docstring example (space.ts:36-50), go-fish, and even BoardSmith's own runner.test.ts fixture game all use `contentsHidden()`/`contentsVisibleToOwner()` in the constructor as the canonical hidden-information mechanism. No lint rule, type, or doc warns that zone visibility is volatile across restore. A reasonable developer following the documented pattern gets hidden hands and deck order broadcast to all players after any undo or server restart, silently. Hidden-information integrity is the core trust property of a board-game engine, so critical severity stands.

title: static visibleAttributes is documented but never enforced — devs who set it believe attributes are hidden when everything is broadcast
trap: `GameElement` declares `static visibleAttributes: string[] | undefined` with the JSDoc 'Attributes visible to all players (undefined = all visible)'. A developer with a card that must show some attributes publicly (e.g. cost on the card back) but hide others (rank) will naturally write `static visibleAttributes = ['cost']` — it autocompletes, compiles, and reads exactly like a security control. But a repo-wide grep shows the field is read nowhere: not in `toJSONForPlayer`, not in `redactHiddenElementAttrs`, not in the session layer. Every attribute of every visible element is serialized to every player regardless; the developer ships a hidden-information leak while believing they opted into protection.
rightWay: The actual controls are zone/element visibility (which hide whole elements, not individual attributes) or the coarse `static playerView` escape hatch (game.ts:459). Attribute-level filtering simply doesn't exist, but the dead field advertises that it does.
suggestion: Either implement it (filter non-listed attributes in `toJSONForPlayer` for non-owners) or delete the declaration entirely — per the repo's own No Backward Compatibility rule, a security-flavored no-op field must not exist. If kept unimplemented even temporarily, make setting it throw at class-registration time.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed: `static visibleAttributes` (game-element.ts:140) is read nowhere — toJSONForPlayer and redactHiddenElementAttrs (game.ts) never consult it; no eslint rule, test, or type constraint guards it. Worse than the claim states, docs/core-concepts.md:137-146 actively teaches the feature with a `secretValue // Hidden from players` example, and line 323 asserts 'Hidden elements show only visibleAttributes' — both false. This is a documented no-op security control, hit by any reasonable dev following the project's own docs. One mitigating nuance: the engine fails SAFE for hidden elements (redactHiddenElementAttrs drops ALL game attributes), so the docs' primary example produces an obvious functional failure rather than a leak; the silent hidden-information leak occurs only when a dev relies on visibleAttributes to strip a secret attribute from a VISIBLE element — realistic given the unqualified JSDoc ('Attributes visible to all players'), but a narrower path than 'everything leaks'. Given a dead security-looking API plus false documentation in a library whose core trust property is hidden-information handling, high severity stands.

title: putInto() accepts the element's own descendant, silently detaching the subtree from the game — elements vanish from all queries and serialization
trap: `moveToInternal` does no self/descendant check. In a stacking game (tokens on tokens, cards under cards) writing `outer.putInto(inner)` where `inner` is inside `outer` — or simply swapping receiver and argument, which type-checks fine since both are Pieces and `destination` is any `GameElement` — creates a 2-node cycle detached from the root. Proven: after the call, the old parent has 0 children, `game.first(Box, 'outer')` returns undefined, and `game.toJSON()` succeeds with the elements simply absent. No error, no dev-mode warning (the tree-corruption detectors in element-collection.ts:337 and piece.ts:88 only catch duplicate-reachability, not detached cycles). The pieces just cease to exist, and the corrupted-but-valid-looking state persists through snapshots.
rightWay: The developer must know to check containment order themselves (`if (!inner.equals(outer) && !outer.all().contains(inner)) ...`) before calling putInto — knowledge nothing in the API surface hints at.
suggestion: In `moveToInternal`, walk `destination._t.parent` up to the root; if `this` is encountered (or `destination === this`), throw an actionable error ('Cannot move X into its own descendant Y'). The walk is O(depth) and matches the fail-fast-and-loud rule.

verdict.reasoning: Empirically confirmed: a vitest repro (outer.create(inner); outer.putInto(inner)) makes both elements vanish from game.first() queries with no error or warning — moveToInternal (piece.ts:80) has no self/descendant check, and the existing dev-mode TREE CORRUPTION detector (piece.ts:88) only catches duplicate-reachability, not detached cycles. No guardrail exists anywhere: docs/common-pitfalls.md never mentions the hazard, the eslint-plugin has no putInto rule, destination is typed as bare GameElement so a receiver/argument swap type-checks, and the command executor path (executor.ts:132) is equally unguarded. The trigger is realistic (piece-on-piece stacking is a documented supported pattern; deck.putInto(card) is a one-swap slip), and the failure mode is silent state loss that serializes cleanly and persists through snapshots — directly contradicting the repo's own 'fail fast and loud' Pit of Success standard, in a function that already demonstrates intent to detect exactly this class of corruption. High severity stands.

title: eachPlayer startingPlayer silently skips players (no wrap-around) — and the docs model the broken dealer pattern
trap: In board games, 'start the round from the player left of the dealer' universally means wrap-around rotation. A dev writes eachPlayer({ startingPlayer: () => game.playerAfterDealer, do: ... }) — exactly what docs/common-patterns.md:54 shows as the canonical dealer-rotation pattern, and what TurnOrder.LEFT_OF_DEALER / START_FROM / CONTINUE (src/engine/flow/turn-order.ts:50,82,131) encode as named presets. But executeEachPlayer builds eligibleSeats via players.slice(startIndex) with no wrap, so every player seated BEFORE the starting player is silently skipped that round. With 4 players and dealer at seat 3, only seat 4 gets a turn. Nothing errors; the round just quietly loses players, and the bug moves around as the dealer rotates.
rightWay: The correct usage is to not use startingPlayer for round-robin at all and instead restructure the flow to handle wrap-around manually (the only hint is a note buried in turn-order.ts JSDoc: 'it does NOT wrap around'). There is no wrapping variant offered, so the right way requires reading engine internals and hand-rolling seat math, while the wrong way is a named preset literally called LEFT_OF_DEALER and the project's own common-patterns doc.
suggestion: Make wrap-around the default: eligibleSeats = [...players.slice(startIndex), ...players.slice(0, startIndex)]. If truncation is ever genuinely wanted, make it an explicit opt-in (e.g. wrap: false). Fix docs/common-patterns.md and the TurnOrder preset docs to match. At minimum, dev-warn when startingPlayer excludes seats.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed in code: engine.ts:1116 builds eligibleSeats via players.slice(startIndex) with no wrap-around, so every player seated before startingPlayer is silently skipped that round. docs/common-patterns.md:54 (the FIRST pattern in the guide, 'Dealer Rotation') models exactly this broken usage with no caveat, and docs/actions-and-flow.md:906 shows TurnOrder.LEFT_OF_DEALER the same way. The trap is amplified by inconsistent semantics: game.nextAfter() (used by the doc's playerAfterDealer) is explicitly circular, while eachPlayer iteration is not. The only warnings live in turn-order.ts JSDoc, not the docs developers read. No guardrails exist: no eslint rule covers it, no tests exercise startingPlayer, and no example game or MERC uses startingPlayer/TurnOrder at all — meaning there's no correct exemplar either. A reasonable developer following the project's own canonical pattern hits silent wrong behavior. Downgraded critical→high because no shipped game is affected (feature is unused everywhere), the symptom (a player never gets a turn) is noticeable in playtesting, and the fix is straightforward — but it remains a genuine, docs-endorsed silent-failure pit.

title: Failed action in simultaneousActionStep is reported as success and recorded in actionHistory
trap: During a simultaneousActionStep (e.g. everyone discards down to 4 cards), a player submits an invalid selection or execute() throws. resumeSimultaneousAction does `if (!result.success) return this.getState();` WITHOUT setting this.actionError — unlike the regular resume path (line 267) which records it. GameRunner.performAction (src/runtime/runner.ts:207) detects failure only via flowState.actionError, so it sees none, returns success:true, and pushes the never-executed action into actionHistory. The client is told the action succeeded, the UI advances, and the replay/undo history now contains an action that never mutated state — replays and snapshots silently diverge.
rightWay: There is no right way from the game dev's side — this is an engine bug in the less-traveled simultaneous path. The regular action-step path handles failure correctly, so devs testing single-player turns will never see it; it only corrupts state in multi-player concurrent phases, which are the hardest to test.
suggestion: In resumeSimultaneousAction, mirror the regular path: set this.actionError = result.error before returning getState(), and clear it on success. Add an engine test that a failed simultaneous action surfaces actionError and is NOT recorded in actionHistory.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED by live reproduction, not just code reading. I built a minimal SimGame whose 'ready' action throws in execute() during a simultaneousActionStep, drove it through GameRunner.performAction (the exact object GameSession.#runner uses at game-session.ts:1303), and observed: execute() threw, no state mutated, yet the runner returned success:true and pushed the never-executed action into actionHistory. Mechanism verified at each layer: (1) ActionExecutor.executeAction (src/engine/action/action.ts:970-979) catches thrown execute() errors and returns {success:false} — so GameRunner's try/catch around continueFlow never fires; (2) FlowEngine.resumeSimultaneousAction (src/engine/flow/engine.ts:457-459) does `if (!result.success) return this.getState();` without setting this.actionError, unlike both sibling paths resume() (line 268) and resumeAfterExternalAction() (line 298) which set it; (3) GameRunner.performAction (src/runtime/runner.ts:207) detects failure solely via flowState.actionError, so it records the action (line 217) and returns success:true. No guardrail exists: nothing in the session layer re-validates, no eslint rule applies (this is engine code, not game code), and there is zero test coverage for a failing action in a simultaneous step (the only failure-adjacent sim test in engine.test.ts covers a 'missing' action name, which throws and IS caught by the runner). The claim's Pit-of-Success framing is accurate: a game dev cannot avoid this — the well-trodden sequential path handles failure correctly, so single-player testing shows nothing wrong; only the hard-to-test concurrent path lies. Severity adjusted from critical to high: the failed action deterministically no-ops on replay too (resumeSimultaneousAction returns before playerDone/completion checks), so snapshots/replays converge rather than diverge as claimed; the concrete harms are the client being told success while server state is unchanged (silent swallowed error, seat still awaiting), polluted actionHistory corrupting undo counting (undo pops a no-op instead of the player's real last move), and per-action checkpoints keyed to inflated history length. Real engine bug, straightforward one-line fix (set this.actionError = result.error in the sim path).

title: chooseFrom multiSelect min/max is client-side only — server accepts any count
trap: A dev writes chooseFrom('cards', { choices: ..., multiSelect: { min: 2, max: 3 } }) (the API is documented in action-builder.ts:224 and used by real games, e.g. demo-action-panel). The AutoUI enforces the bounds (action-metadata.ts ships them to the client), so it looks correct in testing. But validateSelection's choice-type array branch (lines 699-715) only checks membership of each item — it never checks the count. A custom UI calling props.action('discard', { cards: [one] }), a bot, or a hostile client can submit 0, 1, or 50 items and the server validates it, executes, and the execute() handler receives an array of the wrong length.
rightWay: The right way is to also add a .validate() checking value.length — but nothing tells you server enforcement is missing, since the sibling chooseElements type DOES enforce min/max server-side (action.ts:795-807). Two nearly identical multiSelect surfaces, one validated, one not: the dev has no reason to suspect the difference.
suggestion: Port the multiSelect min/max count enforcement from the 'elements' branch (action.ts:795-807) into the 'choice' branch of validateSelection, resolving function-valued multiSelect the same way. Also reject a non-array value when multiSelect is configured.

verdict.reasoning: Verified, could not refute. chooseFrom's multiSelect is a documented first-class API (types.ts:212, action-builder.ts:224), but validateSelection's choice-branch array handling (action.ts:700-715) checks only per-item membership/disabled — no count check — and validate() (action.ts:890-905) has no other gate; the session layer (pick-handler.ts) only ships the min/max config to the client. Decisive evidence: commit 9f38cab ('fix(audit2 F31): enforce chooseElements multiSelect min/max server-side') added exactly this enforcement at action.ts:792-807 but only for the 'elements' selection type — the project's own prior audit judged this vulnerability class real and fix-worthy, and the chooseFrom sibling was simply missed. AutoUI enforces bounds client-side so the gap is invisible in normal testing, and no doc, type, or eslint rule warns of the asymmetry. A custom UI, bot, or hostile client can submit 0 or 50 items and execute() receives a wrong-length array. Severity high matches the F31 precedent.

title: Zone visibility set outside an element-class constructor is silently lost on every snapshot restore — hidden cards come back fully visible after undo, rewind, or server restart
trap: The documented way to hide a zone is imperative: `space.contentsHidden()` / `contentsVisibleToOwner()` / `contentsCountOnly()` in game setup (docs/common-patterns.md, and every reference game does it: go-fish game.ts:56/64, cribbage game.ts:167-189, MERC setup.ts:302-309). But `_zoneVisibility` is in `Space.unserializableAttributes` (src/engine/element/space.ts:117), so `game.toJSON()` never carries it. `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` rebuilds the tree via `loadSerializedState` → `GameElement.fromJSON`, which only re-runs the ELEMENT CLASS constructor. Any zone visibility applied in the Game constructor on a plain Space subclass — or changed at runtime (cribbage flow.ts:222 re-hides the crib mid-game) — evaporates. PROVEN EMPIRICALLY: a Space with `contentsHidden()` at setup redacts its card (`{__hidden:true}`) before restore, and after `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` the same card is served to every player as `{name:'ace', rank:'A'}`. Every restore path hits this: `GameSession.restore()` (server restart), `StateHistory.undoToTurnStart`/`rewindToAction`/`getStateAtAction` (via `GameRunner.fromCheckpoint` → `fromSnapshot`), and the whole stateless `SnapshotSessionHost` path, which reconstructs from the snapshot on EVERY op. The reference games only survive by luck: `Hand`/`Deck` class constructors happen to re-apply their own defaults. A player presses Undo and the opponent's client is broadcast the full contents of a hidden pile — no error, no warning.
rightWay: The only safe pattern is to subclass Space/Deck/Hand and set zone visibility inside the ELEMENT class constructor (as engine `Hand`/`Deck` do), never in game setup and never at runtime. Nothing in the API, types, or docs says this — the docs actively model the fragile pattern, and the codebase itself knows about the hazard (stateless-ops.ts buildSpectatorView comment: 'zone visibility ... is NOT serialized, so a fromSnapshot reconstruction would lose it and over-reveal') but only patched the spectator view, not undo/restore.
suggestion: Serialize `_zoneVisibility` in `Space.toJSON()` and restore it in `GameElement.fromJSON` (it is a small plain object, exactly like the already-serialized element `_visibility`/`json.visibility`). That makes every fromSnapshot path — undo, rewind, restore, stateless ops — visibility-faithful, and makes runtime visibility changes (cribbage crib reveal/re-hide) survive too. Add a regression test mirroring deck-hand-visibility.test.ts that round-trips through getSnapshot/fromSnapshot.

verdict.reasoning: CONFIRMED REAL, with one mitigating factor that lowers it from critical to high. Every load-bearing fact checks out against the code: (1) `_zoneVisibility` is in `Space.unserializableAttributes` (src/engine/element/space.ts:114-118) and, unlike per-element `_visibility` — which IS special-cased into toJSON when explicit (game-element.ts:794, restored at :1027) — zone visibility has no serialization path anywhere (grep of runtime/ and session/ finds none). (2) `GameRunner.fromSnapshot` (src/runtime/runner.ts:535-600) calls `game.loadSerializedState`, which discards the constructor-built tree (`this._t.children = []`, game.ts:2849) and rebuilds via `GameElement.fromJSON`, re-running only element-class constructors. (3) I reproduced it empirically with a fresh test: a plain Space with `contentsHidden()` serves its card to an opponent as `{__hidden:true}` before restore and as `{name:'ace',rank:'A'}` after `fromSnapshot` — a silent full reveal, no error. (4) The codebase self-incriminates: src/session/stateless-ops.ts:220 explicitly says zone visibility 'is NOT serialized, so a fromSnapshot reconstruction would lose it and over-reveal' — but only the spectator view was patched, not undo/rewind/restore. (5) No guardrail exists: no eslint rule (src/eslint-plugin/rules/ has nothing visibility-related), no docs warning; docs actively model the fragile pattern, including hiding a PLAIN Space imperatively (docs/common-pitfalls.md:699 `this.stashZone = this.create(Space, 'stash'); this.stashZone.contentsHidden()` — exactly the leaking case). A reasonable developer following the docs hits this. Why not critical: the dominant hidden-zone use cases — Hand and Deck — are secure by class-constructor default (`setZoneVisibility('owner')` in hand.ts:55, `'hidden'` in deck.ts:60), so all reference games' hands/draw-piles survive restore safely (go-fish Pond extends Deck; cribbage Crib extends Deck, and its runtime visibility changes fail in the SAFE direction — the crib comes back hidden, an under-reveal UX bug, not a leak). The over-reveal requires a plain Space/Grid hidden imperatively (documented but less common than hands/decks) or `hideContentsFrom`/`addZoneVisibleTo` at runtime. So it is a genuine, empirically proven, silent information-leak pit with zero guardrails — real and severe — but its practical blast radius is narrower than 'every hidden zone in every game', which is what critical would imply. The correct fix direction (serialize explicit zone visibility like per-element `_visibility` already is) is also evident from the existing special-case at game-element.ts:794.

title: state.players broadcasts every custom Player attribute (and any Player-child elements) unfiltered to all seats and spectators — a parallel channel that bypasses the entire visibility system
trap: The natural place to store per-player secrets is the Player subclass every game already has (`class MyPlayer extends Player { secretRole = '' }` — same shape as go-fish's `bookCount`). The board `view` is diligently filtered per-seat via `toJSONForPlayer`, but `buildPlayerState` separately builds `state.players` by calling raw `player.toJSON()` for ALL players and flattening `attributes` to the root — no viewer parameter, no visibility check, sent identically to every seat and spectator on every broadcast (game-session.ts:2120) and via the stateless `buildViews` (stateless-ops.ts:212). PROVEN EMPIRICALLY: seat 2's `state.players` contains seat 1's `secretRole: 'traitor'`. Even a defensive author who calls `player.hideFromAll()` or element-level visibility is still leaked here, because this path never consults `isVisibleTo`. And because `player.toJSON()` includes `children`, a dev who parents a hand under the player (`player.create(Hand, ...)` — compiles fine, feels idiomatic) ships the full unfiltered hand contents in `players[i].children`.
rightWay: Secrets must live on elements inside visibility-managed zones, never as Player attributes — but nothing enforces or documents this, and the filtered `view` sitting right next to the unfiltered `players` array in the same PlayerGameState makes the two look equally safe.
suggestion: Route the players array through the same filter as the view: either build it from `toJSONForPlayer(playerPosition)`'s Player nodes, or apply `isVisibleTo(viewer)`/attribute redaction per player and drop `children` entirely (the UI only needs flattened attributes). Alternatively make hidden-by-default explicit: only serialize a whitelisted set (name, seat, color, colorLabel) plus attributes the game opts in via something like `static publicAttributes`.

verdict.reasoning: Empirically reproduced (temp vitest test, since deleted): buildPlayerState (src/session/utils.ts:237) calls raw player.toJSON() for all players with no viewer parameter and flattens attributes to root; seat 2 AND the spectator received players[0].secretRole='traitor', and a player-parented hand created with contentsVisibleToOwner() shipped full card identity (name+value) in state.players[0].children while the adjacent filtered `view` correctly anonymized the same card (__hidden, id -4000). This is the production broadcast path (game-session.ts broadcast loop) and stateless-ops buildViews/buildSpectatorView. Refutation attempts all failed: (a) docs/core-concepts.md documents `static visibleAttributes` as the attribute-visibility mechanism, but grep shows it is declared at game-element.ts:140 and never consulted anywhere in src — setting it had zero effect (the attribute even leaks in the filtered view's player node); (b) no eslint-plugin rule covers this (only no-network/no-timers/etc.); (c) no doc warns against secrets on Player — on the contrary, every example game subclasses Player with custom attributes read from state.players (go-fish bookCount), making secretRole the obvious next step for a hidden-role game; (d) Player has no hideFromAll/showOnlyTo (Piece-only), so a defensive author has no API to reach for. Only mitigation: reference games happen to parent hands under game rather than player, so no shipped game leaks today — but that is convention, not a guardrail. Given the library's heavy anti-cheat investment elsewhere (anonymized ids, SEC-02 sweeps, image redaction), this is a genuine parallel unfiltered channel; severity high is warranted.

title: boardsmith.json playerCount is silently dead config — gameDefinition always wins, and the scaffold hardcodes both
trap: The scaffold writes `"playerCount": { "min": 2, "max": 4 }` into boardsmith.json (project-scaffold.ts:109) — the file docs call "Game configuration" and the file `boardsmith validate` checks. A dev who wants a 2-6 player game naturally edits boardsmith.json. Nothing changes: dev.ts:358-359 resolves `minPlayers = gameDefinition.minPlayers ?? config.playerCount?.min ?? config.minPlayers ?? 2`, and the scaffold ALSO hardcodes minPlayers/maxPlayers into src/rules/index.ts's gameDefinition (project-scaffold.ts:244-245), so the JSON value is never consulted. Worse, the published manifest.json is a copy of boardsmith.json (build.ts:107), so the platform lobby can advertise 2-6 while the shipped rules and dev host enforce 2-4 — a dev/prod divergence with no warning anywhere.
rightWay: The real source of truth is gameDefinition in src/rules/index.ts, which the developer has no reason to suspect duplicates the JSON. Discovering this requires reading dev.ts's precedence chain. The chain also accepts three spellings (playerCount.{min,max}, top-level minPlayers/maxPlayers, gameDefinition) — two of them silently losing.
suggestion: Pick ONE source of truth. Either the scaffold's gameDefinition should read boardsmith.json (import the JSON) so there is literally one place to edit, or dev/validate should error loudly when boardsmith.json playerCount disagrees with gameDefinition.minPlayers/maxPlayers instead of silently preferring one.

verdict.reasoning: Every factual claim verified. project-scaffold.ts:109 writes playerCount into boardsmith.json while lines 244-245 hardcode the same values into the generated gameDefinition; dev.ts:358-359's precedence chain (gameDefinition ?? config.playerCount ?? config.minPlayers ?? default) means the JSON value is dead config for all scaffolded projects. build.ts:107 copies the JSON (including playerCount) into the published manifest.json, and zip.ts requires it, so editing either copy produces silent dev/prod divergence. No guardrails: validate.ts checks the JSON's playerCount internal consistency but never cross-checks gameDefinition; no eslint rule applies; docs actively mislead — getting-started.md shows playerCount as boardsmith.json 'Game Configuration' and core-concepts.md claims boardsmith.json is the 'single source of truth' for lobby config while playerCount is the one lobby-shaped field not read from it. Example games (hex, go-fish) duplicate the values in both places, kept in sync only by discipline. A reasonable dev widening player count edits one copy, local dev either silently ignores it (JSON edit) or works while the published manifest stays stale (gameDefinition edit); build/validate/publish all pass. Severity stays high: the divergence is invisible locally, uncaught by any tool, and surfaces as a production platform-lobby mismatch, directly violating the project's own single-source-of-truth and fail-fast principles.

title: onEnter/onExit handlers registered in the game constructor silently stop firing after any snapshot restore
trap: The Space class docstring (space.ts:52-55) models registering reactive rules in setup: `discardPile.onEnter((card) => game.message(...), Card)`. `_eventHandlers` is unserializable (correctly — they're closures), but `loadSerializedState` throws away the constructor-created Space instances that hold them and rebuilds fresh ones from JSON with empty handler lists. Proven: a handler fired before restore and never fired again after `loadSerializedState` + `putInto`. Game logic hung on enter/exit events (auto-scoring, triggered messages, cleanup) silently degrades after undo/server-restore, with no warning that handlers evaporated.
rightWay: Handlers would survive only if re-registered after restore, but there is no post-restore hook on Game for doing so; the only safe pattern is to avoid onEnter/onExit for anything rules-critical and put the logic in action execute callbacks instead — the opposite of what the docstring example teaches.
suggestion: Either re-bind handlers on restore (e.g. a `setupElements()` template method that loadSerializedState re-invokes on the rebuilt tree, with visibility/handlers applied there), or dev-warn when loadSerializedState discards a Space that had registered handlers, and fix the docstring to scope onEnter to restore-safe uses.

verdict.reasoning: Empirically reproduced: a handler registered per the Space docstring pattern fired before loadSerializedState and never after (fired before: 1, after: 0). Mechanism confirmed in code: loadSerializedState (src/engine/element/game.ts:2848-2857) discards constructor-created Space instances (this._t.children = []) and rebuilds via GameElement.fromJSON, which constructs fresh instances whose _eventHandlers is empty (unserializableAttributes, space.ts:114-118); nothing re-registers. This restore primitive backs GameRunner.fromSnapshot and therefore undo (state-history.ts:362), server restore (game-session.ts:785), and stateless-ops (stateless-ops.ts:798) — all core paths, not contrived. No guardrails exist: the only documentation of onEnter/onExit anywhere in the repo is the Space docstring itself, which teaches the exact broken pattern; no eslint rule, no docs warning, no post-restore hook on Game. Mitigating factor keeping severity at medium rather than high: no shipped game (reference games or MERC) currently uses onEnter/onExit, so there is no live breakage — but a reasonable dev following the class docs would hit silent rules-logic loss after any undo or server restart, the classic Pit-of-Failure (works in initial testing, silently degrades later).

title: docs/core-concepts.md teaches an event-sourcing command model that no longer exists, including a nonexistent element.setAttribute() API

title: resolveArgs silently converts ANY numeric non-selection arg into a GameElement

title: forEach re-evaluates a dynamic collection every iteration against a stored numeric index — mutating the collection skips items
trap: executeForEach calls config.collection(context) fresh on EVERY iteration and indexes it with the persisted itemIndex. The natural usage — forEach({ collection: ctx => ctx.player.hand.all(Card), as: 'card', do: <step that plays/moves the card> }) — shrinks the array each iteration, so the classic index-into-mutating-array bug applies: every other card is silently skipped, and the loop 'completes' normally. rightWay: The right way is to snapshot the collection first (setVar with a copied array, or pass a static array), but nothing in the forEach docs or types says the collection function is re-invoked per iteration; a reader reasonably assumes it is evaluated once like a normal for-of.
suggestion: Evaluate the collection once on first entry and store a stable identity list in frame.data (element ids for GameElements, mirroring eachPlayer's eligibleSeats snapshot), or at minimum devWarn when the collection's length/identity changes between iterations.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed real. executeForEach (src/engine/flow/engine.ts:1157-1176) calls `config.collection(context)` fresh on every re-entry of the frame and indexes it with the persisted `itemIndex` — so a collection callback backed by a live element query that shrinks as the `do` body moves/removes items will silently skip every other item, and the loop still "completes" normally. Attempts to refute failed on every front: (1) No documentation warns of per-iteration re-evaluation — docs/actions-and-flow.md's forEach section and the builder JSDoc (src/engine/flow/builders.ts:157-168) say nothing about it; worse, the builder's own @example is `collection: (ctx) => ctx.game.all(Card), as: 'card', do: actionStep({...})` — a live query with a player-action body, actively steering developers toward the risky pattern. (2) No lint rule covers it — src/eslint-plugin/rules/ has no-element-array-state, no-element-identity-comparison, no-network, etc., nothing about flow collections. (4) The engine's own sibling primitive proves the authors know better: executeEachPlayer snapshots `eligibleSeats` into frame.data on first entry (engine.ts:1114-1118) precisely to avoid this, so forEach's behavior is an internal inconsistency, not a deliberate documented semantic. Mitigating factors keeping it at medium rather than high: all real usages found in docs/games iterate stable collections (players, show order), the mutating-body pattern is a secondary rather than the single most common path, and re-evaluation is partly forced by frame.data serializability (element references can't be persisted) — but eachPlayer shows a serializable-ID snapshot solution exists. title: Custom-UI action failures are completely silent: lastError has zero consumers and start() returns void
trap: The docs (docs/custom-ui-guide.md:120, :141, :242) and every reference game model fire-and-forget calls: `await actionController.execute('endTurn')`, `actionController.start('retreat')` (hex/HexBoard.vue:120 ignores the result too). When the action is unavailable, it's not your turn, or the server rejects it, `start()` just sets `lastError` and returns void (lines 1252-1255, 1260-1262) and `execute()` returns a result object nobody is told to check. `grep lastError` across src/ui shows NOTHING outside the controller reads it — no toast, no panel banner. The player clicks, nothing happens, no console output, no UI feedback.

Meanwhile the SAME action failing through the auto ActionPanel path DOES show a toast (src/ui/components/auto-ui/ActionPanel.vue:745), so parity between Custom UI and Action Panel is broken exactly on the error path.

Additionally make `start()` return `Promise<ActionResult|ValidationResult>` so failure is at least detectable, and devWarn when `start()` is called for an unavailable action.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: lastError (src/ui/composables/useActionController.ts) has zero consumers in shipped UI — only the controller, tests, and the type export reference it; GameShell toasts undo/hint/lobby errors but never custom-UI action failures. start() returns void and silently sets lastError on unavailable-action/no-metadata (lines 1252-1262); execute() failure sets lastError with no console output, and dispatchActionResolved is dev-build-only (erased in production). ActionPanel.vue (~line 745) toasts the identical failure in the Auto UI path, so Custom-UI/ActionPanel error-path parity — an explicit repo rule — is genuinely broken. Reference game hex (HexBoard.vue:120) ignores the execute result, and no game in ~/BoardSmithGames reads lastError, so the modeled easy path is fire-and-forget with silent failure. However, the claim overstates two things: the docs DO document the correct patterns (custom-ui-guide.md:129-131 checks result.success; :733-736 shows watching lastError; :878-879 renders lastError in a template), just not in the primary examples; and well-gated custom UIs (clicks only offered when the action is available/it's your turn) make production failures edge cases (races, stale state) rather than the everyday flow, with dev builds retaining DebugPanel + the action-resolved event for diagnosis. Real pit-of-success violation ("fail fast and loud" is the repo's own rule), but mitigations lower it from high to medium.

title: fill() accepts a scalar for a multiSelect pick and submits it — no guard, asymmetric with toggleMultiSelect
trap: For a `chooseElements`/multiSelect pick, the natural first attempt is `await actionController.fill('cards', cardId)` — the same call used for every other pick type and the one the docs teach (custom-ui-guide.md:316). `fill()` never consults the selection's multiSelect config: `validateSelection` happily matches the scalar against the choices list, `currentArgs['cards']` becomes a number, `isReady` flips true, and auto-execute submits a scalar where the engine expects an array — failing server-side with a confusing engine error (or, per the previous finding, silently). `toggleMultiSelect` has the reverse guard (line 1729 devWarns 'not a multiSelect selection... use fill()'), but fill has no 'this IS a multiSelect... use toggleMultiSelect()' counterpart.
rightWay: The correct path is `toggleMultiSelect(name, value)` + `confirmMultiSelect()` (or fill with a complete array), which is only discoverable by reading cribbage's source or the controller internals — the shared-draft parity mechanism (multiSelectDraft) is invisible from fill()'s signature.
suggestion: In fill(), when the selection resolves to a multiSelect config and the value is not an array, devWarn (or auto-wrap with a warning): 'selection X is multiSelect (min/max) — use toggleMultiSelect()/confirmMultiSelect() or pass an array', mirroring the existing guard in toggleMultiSelect.

verdict.reasoning: Verified in code: fill() (useActionController.ts:1311) never consults the selection's multiSelect config, while toggleMultiSelect has the reverse-direction devWarn guard (line 1731) — the asymmetry is real. Client validateSelection matches a scalar against per-element choices and auto-execute submits it. Engine side (action.ts:792-807) treats a scalar as count=1: with multiSelect min>=2 the dev gets a count error that never mentions toggleMultiSelect; with min=1 the scalar PASSES validation and execute() receives a single GameElement where the typed args promise an array — a silent type lie with no normalization. Docs make the trap the easy path: custom-ui-guide.md teaches fill(name, card.id) for element clicks (line 316) and contains zero mentions of toggleMultiSelect/confirmMultiSelect; the only example is cribbage's source. Mitigation exists only for UIs using useBoardActionBridge's click routing, but the guide explicitly teaches the manual onClick+fill pattern. No lint rule covers it. A reasonable developer following the docs hits this on their first multiSelect pick. Dev-time only and fails fast, so medium severity stands.

title: Zoom container's width:max-content silently collapses responsive custom boards (percentage widths / container-type) to zero
trap: The Vue/CSS-idiomatic way to build a responsive board is `width: 100%` (or `container-type: inline-size` + container queries) on the board root. GameShell mounts the #game-board slot inside `.game-shell__zoom-container { width: max-content }` (line 2822), so a percentage-width board has no definite containing width and collapses; `container-type` collapses it to 0 outright. Nothing warns: useAutoZoom's `measureAndFit` treats a <1px board as 'not laid out yet' (useAutoZoom.ts:36) and just keeps waiting forever, and the custom-UI guide contains no sizing guidance at all (no mention of max-content, boardregion measurement, or container-type). The developer sees a blank board area with no error. This exact trap has already bitten the project itself (custom-UI responsive sizing).
rightWay: The working pattern — give the board an intrinsic (fixed or content-derived) size, or measure `.boardregion` yourself and pin an explicit pixel width — is undocumented and contradicts standard responsive-CSS instincts.
suggestion: Add a dev-mode check: once game state has arrived and the slot has children, if the zoom container measures ~0×0 (or the board root has a percentage width/container-type under max-content sizing), console.error an actionable message ('board collapsed under max-content sizing — give it an intrinsic size; see custom-ui-guide § board sizing'). verdict.reasoning: Confirmed real. GameShell.vue's zoom container does use width:max-content (intentional for the zoom/scroll design), under which a percentage-width board root collapses and container-type:inline-size collapses to 0. The failure is fully silent: useAutoZoom's computeFitZoom treats <1px as 'not laid out yet' and waits forever with no warning. No guardrails exist anywhere: docs/custom-ui-guide.md and common-pitfalls.md contain zero board-sizing guidance, and the eslint-plugin rules are all engine-determinism rules (no-network/no-timers), nothing CSS-related. Reference games avoid the trap only incidentally (hex: width:fit-content + computed SVG width; checkers: min(80vw,480px); go-fish's width:100% root survives via fixed-px card children) — none teach the safe pattern. Dispositively, the project's own memory ('Custom-UI responsive sizing') records the maintainers themselves hitting this exact trap (container-type collapsing the board to 0; workaround of measuring .boardregion and pinning a pixel width), and that knowledge lives only in agent memory, not docs. A reasonable developer following standard responsive-CSS instincts (width:100% or container queries) hits a blank board with no error. Severity stays medium: it's a silent DX trap with an undocumented workaround, not a correctness bug in shipped games, and the max-content design itself is justified; fix is cheap (docs section + dev-mode warning when the board stays <1px past settle).

title: No way to await GameConnection becoming open — actions sent immediately after connect() silently fail with a resolved {success:false}
trap: The natural sequence is `const conn = client.connect(gameId); const res = await conn.action('move', args)`. `MeepleClient.connect()` (client.ts:171-186) synchronously fires `connection.connect()` and returns, and `GameConnection.action()` at line 128-131 checks `readyState !== OPEN` and RESOLVES `{ success: false, error: 'Not connected' }` instead of rejecting. So the await succeeds, no exception is thrown, and unless the dev remembers to check `.success` the move just vanishes. The library's own Vue composable proves the trap is real: src/client/vue.ts:120-122 papers over it with `setTimeout(() => { isSettingUp = false }, 100) // allow connection to establish` — a timing hack inside the SDK itself.
rightWay: The correct pattern is to register `onConnectionChange` and only act once status === 'connected' — a callback dance nobody writes for a one-shot script. The repo already knows the right design: the sibling `createDevHostClient` (src/client/dev-host-client.ts:112, 171-179) exposes an `opened: Promise<void>` and THROWS 'Await `client.opened` before sending' on a not-open send. GameConnection, the production client, has neither.
suggestion: Give GameConnection an `opened`/`connected` Promise (mirroring dev-host-client) and make `MeepleClient.connect()` either async (resolving when open) or return the promise alongside the connection. Have `action()` before open either await the open or reject loudly, instead of resolving a success:false result. Then delete the setTimeout(100) hack in vue.ts.

verdict.reasoning: Every element of the claim checks out. game-connection.ts:128-131 resolves {success:false, error:'Not connected'} instead of rejecting when the socket isn't open, and MeepleClient.connect() (client.ts:171-186) returns synchronously while the socket is still CONNECTING — so the natural `connect(); await action()` sequence silently drops the action unless the caller inspects .success. GameConnection offers no awaitable open signal (only callback-based onConnectionChange), and the SDK's own Vue composable (vue.ts:119-122) papers over the race with a `setTimeout(..., 100) // allow connection to establish` hack — internal proof the trap is real. The repo already codified the correct design in the sibling dev-host-client.ts (readonly opened: Promise<void>, and a thrown 'Await client.opened before sending' on not-open send), so this is a known-right pattern missing from the production client. Worse, docs/api/client.md's quickstart (lines 72-87) shows exactly the trap sequence — connect then await action — so documentation reinforces rather than guards the wrong path; no lint rule covers it. Severity adjusted from high to medium: the failure is deterministic and surfaces on the very first action of any script (with an error string in the resolved result for anyone who checks), typical browser UI usage triggers actions via user clicks well after connect, and no data corruption occurs — it's a first-run DX trap in the SDK's primary verb, not a latent production hazard.

title: disconnect() permanently disables auto-reconnect; a later connect() silently leaves it off — only the differently-named reconnect() restores it
trap: `disconnect()` (line 99-103) mutates `this.config.autoReconnect = false` as an implementation trick to suppress reconnection. `connect()` (line 81) never restores it — only `reconnect()` (line 105-110) does. A dev who pairs the obviously-symmetric `conn.disconnect()` / `conn.connect()` (e.g. pause on tab-hide, resume on tab-show) gets a connection that works until the first network blip, then never auto-reconnects despite having configured `autoReconnect: true`. The Vue composable steps straight into this: `useGame` with `autoConnect: false` (vue.ts:141-144) creates the connection (which immediately starts a WS handshake it then kills) and calls `connection.disconnect()` — so the user-facing `connect()` it returns (vue.ts:195-197) always produces a connection with auto-reconnect silently disabled.
rightWay: Call `reconnect()` instead of `connect()` after a `disconnect()` — nothing in the method names or docs suggests `connect()` is the wrong resume path; the mutation of user config inside disconnect() is invisible.
suggestion: Track suppression in a separate private flag (`#userDisconnected`) instead of mutating `config.autoReconnect`, and have `connect()` clear it. Also give GameConnectionConfig an explicit `connectImmediately` option so `useGame({ autoConnect: false })` doesn't open-and-kill a socket.

verdict.reasoning: Verified in code: disconnect() (game-connection.ts:100) mutates user config (autoReconnect=false) as its suppression trick; connect() never restores it and scheduleReconnect() (line 338) bails on the flag, so a disconnect()/connect() pair silently loses auto-reconnect forever. The library's own Vue composable hits this exact trap: useGame with autoConnect:false passes autoReconnect:true (vue.ts:116) then calls connection.disconnect() (vue.ts:142), and its exposed connect() (vue.ts:196) calls connection.connect() — so every autoConnect:false consumer gets auto-reconnect permanently disabled. No JSDoc, no docs (docs/api/client.md never mentions reconnect()), no lint rule, and no test guards the asymmetry. This is not contrived misuse — pairing the symmetric names is the easy path, and it fails silently only after the first network blip. Severity medium is appropriate: silent latent degradation, but manually recoverable and no data corruption.

title: MeepleClient methods are split between throw-on-failure and return-raw-JSON — half the lobby API silently returns failures
trap: `findMatch`, `getGameState`, `performAction`, `getHistory`, `restartGame`, `getLobby`, `updateLobbyName` all check `data.success` and THROW with the server's error. But `createGame` (line 215-222), `claimSeat` (336-347), `joinLobby` (352-362), `setReady`, `addSlot`, `removeSlot`, `setSlotAI`, `leavePosition`, `kickPlayer`, `updatePlayerOptions`, `updateSlotPlayerOptions`, `updateGameOptions` just `return await response.json()`. A dev calibrated by `performAction` throwing will write `const { gameId } = await client.createGame(...)` — on failure gameId is undefined, no error surfaces, and the bug shows up later as a confusing 'No game ID' or a connect to `games/undefined`. There is no signal which category a method is in except reading its body.
rightWay: For the raw-JSON half you must check `.success` on every result; for the throwing half you must try/catch. Knowing which is which requires reading the SDK source — the type signatures don't distinguish them (both are async and the response types happen to include `success`).
suggestion: Pick one contract for the whole client (Pit of Success says: throw with ErrorCode on `!data.success`, and also on non-2xx HTTP where `response.json()` currently throws an unrelated parse error). If lobby methods must return `LobbyResponse` for flow control, at least make all of them do so — including createGame, whose failure is never a normal flow outcome.

verdict.reasoning: Verified in src/client/client.ts: 6 methods (getGameState, performAction, getHistory, restartGame, getLobby, updateLobbyName) check data.success and throw, while 12 others (createGame, claimSeat, joinLobby, setReady, addSlot, removeSlot, setSlotAI, leavePosition, kickPlayer, updatePlayerOptions, updateSlotPlayerOptions, updateGameOptions) return raw JSON; the private fetch helper also never checks response.ok. Critically, the SDK's own docs (docs/api/client.md lines 65 and 206) demonstrate the exact trap: `const { gameId } = await client.createGame(...)` then `client.connect(gameId)` with no success check — the documented easy path IS the failure path. Guardrails are weak: CreateGameResponse.gameId is optional (helps only strict-TS users, and the doc example wouldn't even compile), LobbyResponse methods have zero type signal so awaited fire-and-forget calls silently swallow server rejections, no eslint-plugin rule applies (those target game determinism), and no discriminated union forces the check. First-party GameShell.vue defensively does BOTH try/catch and .success checks, confirming even internal code can't tell which discipline a method uses. Not contrived — a reasonable dev calibrated by performAction or by the docs hits this. Medium severity is appropriate: real silent-failure inconsistency in the public SDK, but scoped to HTTP lobby/setup calls (gameplay mostly flows over WebSocket) with a partial type nudge on createGame.

title: Client SDK redefines protocol types instead of importing the canonical ones — and they have already drifted (CreateGameRequest lost playerIds; WS messages lost the discriminated union)
trap: protocol.ts's header commands 'Import from here rather than defining these types elsewhere', yet src/client/types.ts redefines `CreateGameRequest` (line 288), `ClaimSeatRequest` (330), `SetReadyRequest`/`AddSlotRequest`/etc (360-394), and replaces the canonical discriminated WS union with loose bags: `WebSocketOutgoingMessage` (237-243) and `WebSocketIncomingMessage` (245-276) where every field is optional — exactly the invalid-states-representable shape protocol.ts exists to prevent. The drift is already real: the client `CreateGameRequest` is missing `playerIds?: string[]` present in the protocol version (protocol.ts:217), so a dev who imports from 'boardsmith/client' (the natural import when using MeepleClient) cannot pass playerIds that the wire format supports — and which import you get depends on auto-import luck between two identically-named types.
rightWay: Know that 'boardsmith/types' is canonical and hand-pick imports from there even while working against the client SDK, ignoring the same-named types the SDK's own methods are typed with.
suggestion: Delete the duplicated request types from client/types.ts and re-export from ../types/protocol.js (as it already does for the Lobby types at line 327). Replace WebSocketOutgoingMessage with the canonical `WebSocketMessage` union narrowed to the client-sent variants, and make WebSocketIncomingMessage a discriminated union keyed on type.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: protocol.ts's header declares it the single source of truth and forbids redefining these types elsewhere, yet src/client/types.ts redefines CreateGameRequest (288), ClaimSeatRequest (330), the lobby request types (360-394), and flattens the canonical discriminated WebSocketMessage union (protocol.ts:420) into all-optional bags (237-276). MeepleClient.createGame() is typed against the stale client copy (client.ts:215), so TypeScript's excess-property check blocks a developer on the natural 'boardsmith/client' import path from passing a wire-supported field. No guardrail exists: eslint-plugin rules cover game-code determinism only, and the file itself shows the half-applied fix (line 327 re-exports lobby state types from the canonical source while the request types remain forked).
