title: switchOn with no default silently no-ops on an unmatched value
trap: executeSwitch stringifies config.on(ctx) and looks it up in cases; if there is no matching case and no default, it marks the frame completed and continues (lines 1387-1392). A typo'd case key, a new enum value added later, or a value that stringifies unexpectedly ('undefined', '[object Object]') means an entire flow branch is silently skipped mid-game — the flow just moves on with no warning.
rightWay: The right way is to always provide a default or keep cases exhaustive, but the type system can't enforce string-keyed exhaustiveness and the engine gives zero signal when it falls through — the dev only notices when the game behaves wrong turns later.
suggestion: When no case matches and no default exists, throw (or at minimum devWarn) with the stringified value and the available case keys: "switchOn 'phase' got 'combatt' — no matching case (draw, play, combat) and no default".

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed: executeSwitch (src/engine/flow/engine.ts:1384-1392) silently completes the frame when config.on(ctx) stringifies to an unmatched key and no default exists — no warning, no error. Nothing in the type system (on returns unknown, cases is Record<string, FlowNode>) or src/eslint-plugin/ guards this, and the failure mode (silently skipped flow branch discovered turns later) conflicts with the project's own 'fail fast and loud' rule; the new-enum-value-added-later scenario is realistic. However, severity is downgraded to low: the behavior exactly mirrors JavaScript switch semantics so it matches reasonable developer expectations; the optional-default no-op is an intentional, tested API (engine.test.ts:506) that legitimately supports 'branch only on some values'; the docs example (docs/actions-and-flow.md) shows default provided; and no game in ~/BoardSmithGames/ or MERC uses switchOn at all, so real-world exposure is currently zero. A dev-mode warning or a lint rule requiring default would close the gap cheaply, but this is a minor design nit, not a medium-severity trap.

title: Action builder ships a default no-op execute; .build() returns a fully registerable silent-success action
trap: The builder's constructor initializes execute: () => {} (line 77), and .build() (line 636-640, doc'd 'without execute, for inspection') returns the same ActionDefinition type as .execute(). A dev who ends a chain with .build() — a plausible reading of 'finish building the action' — gets an action that registers fine, validates selections, reports success to the player, and does absolutely nothing. The invalid state 'action with no handler' is representable and indistinguishable at the type level from a real action.
rightWay: The right way is to terminate every chain with .execute(fn); the only protection is that forgetting BOTH execute and build is a compile error (Action isn't ActionDefinition). But .build() looks like the terminal method and produces the silent no-op.
suggestion: Remove the default no-op: have .build() return a definition flagged as handler-less and make registerAction() throw an actionable error for it ("action 'x' has no execute handler — end the chain with .execute(fn)"). Or rename build() to inspectDefinition() and make its return type non-assignable to ActionDefinition.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: the constructor seeds execute: () => {} (action-builder.ts:77) and build() (:638) returns the same ActionDefinition type as execute(), so a .build()-terminated action registers, validates, reports success, and silently does nothing — the invalid state is representable and type-indistinguishable. Refutation attempts failed: .build() has ZERO call sites anywhere (src, tests, docs, ~/BoardSmithGames), so it isn't a used inspection hook; no eslint rule or runtime guard covers it; the type system's forced-terminal-call protection is exactly what makes build() satisfy the checker like execute() does. Docs universally end chains with .execute() and build()'s docstring says 'for inspection', but 'build()' is the canonical terminal name in builder patterns, so autocomplete makes it a plausible easy-path pick. Downgraded to low because the symptom (action does nothing) surfaces on first playtest rather than corrupting state latently, and the fix is trivial under the repo's no-backward-compat rule: delete the dead method or return a non-ActionDefinition inspection type.

title: session.runner.performAction() is one property away from session.performAction() but silently skips persistence, broadcast, checkpoints, tutorials, and AI scheduling
trap: GameSession publicly exposes `get runner()` ('for advanced use cases') and GameRunner has a method with the exact same name and signature as the session's: `performAction(action, player, args)`. A dev scripting a bot, a test harness, or a server hook will naturally call `session.runner.performAction(...)` — it succeeds, mutates real game state, and returns a success result. But nothing saves (the persisted snapshot is now stale — a restart rolls the move back), nothing broadcasts (clients silently desync), no undo checkpoint is refreshed at the right boundary, tutorials don't auto-advance, and AI opponents never wake up. The game just looks 'stuck' for other players with zero errors anywhere.
rightWay: Always call `session.performAction(...)` and treat `runner` as read-only. The docstrings don't say the runner's mutation methods are off-limits when a session owns it, and the identical method name makes the wrong call read as correct in review.
suggestion: Don't expose the raw runner from GameSession: return a read-only facade (state/view/history getters only), or rename the runner-level method (e.g. `executeActionUnmanaged`) so the two paths can't be confused. At minimum have GameRunner.performAction warn when the runner is owned by a session.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: GameSession.performAction (game-session.ts:1294) wraps runner.performAction and then persists (#save), captures checkpoints, broadcasts, auto-advances tutorials, and schedules AI; GameRunner.performAction (runtime/runner.ts:154) does none of that, yet `get runner()` (game-session.ts:832, 'for advanced use cases') exposes the fully mutable runner with no docstring warning, no readonly type, and no eslint-plugin rule (those rules target game-code determinism, not session API misuse). The confusion is not contrived: docs/api/runtime.md and docs/agent-control.md:174 explicitly show `runner.performAction(...)` as the in-process submission path for standalone/TestGame contexts, so a dev porting bot/harness code into a session-hosted context would plausibly carry it over, and the failure is silent divergence (stale snapshot, client desync, AI never wakes) — the project already hit a cousin of this (v4.4 SnapshotSessionHost dual-wiring trap). Severity adjusted down to low because the genuinely easy path is the correct one — session.performAction is the method shown in docs/api/session.md, the GameSession header example, and agent-control.md:439; the wrong call requires deliberately reaching through an accessor labeled 'advanced'; the signatures differ (async Promise<ActionResult> vs sync), giving some type-level friction; the audience is narrow (host/test implementers, not game devs); and every internal use of session.runner in the repo is read-only. Real footgun worth a docstring warning or read-only surface, but not a trap a reasonable developer on the path of least resistance falls into.

title: dragProps() silently ignores the documented `when` option — element stays draggable
trap: `dragProps(ref, options?: DragOptions)` accepts `DragOptions`, whose `when` field is documented as "Condition for enabling drag." The file's own '## Full API (for advanced use)' section models `v-bind="dragProps({ id: card.id })"`. A dev on the full API who writes `dragProps({ id: card.id }, { when: canDrag(card.id) })` gets code that compiles and type-checks — but `dragProps` never reads `options.when` (only `onDragStart`/`onDragEnd`), so it unconditionally returns `draggable: true` with live handlers. Disabled cards remain draggable; drags fire `startDrag` and can auto-START an action via the drag orchestration (useDragDropTargets.ts Case B) that the UI author explicitly tried to gate off.
rightWay: Only the `drag()` wrapper (line 324) evaluates `when` and returns `{}` props when false. Nothing tells you the sibling function with the identical options type behaves differently — the two ways look interchangeable and the wrong one fails silently.
suggestion: Make `dragProps` honor `when` (return `{ draggable: false }`-style inert props or check the condition inside onDragstart), or narrow its signature to `Pick<DragOptions,'onDragStart'|'onDragEnd'>` so passing `when` is a type error.

verdict.reasoning: Verified in src/ui/composables/useDragDrop.ts: dragProps (line 212) accepts options?: DragOptions but only reads onDragStart/onDragEnd; DragOptions.when (line 127, JSDoc "Condition for enabling drag") is silently ignored and dragProps unconditionally returns draggable: true with live startDrag handlers. Only drag() (line 324) evaluates when via evalCondition. Since the options parameter legitimately exists on dragProps (for lifecycle callbacks) and IDE autocomplete shows the shared DragOptions type with its "Condition for enabling drag" doc, writing dragProps(ref, { when: ... }) is a natural, type-checking mistake that fails with zero feedback — a genuine Pit of Success violation by the repo's own standards, and no eslint-plugin rule or dev warning guards it. Downgraded to low, though: (1) docs/ui-components.md documents dragProps as (ref)-only, marks it "Low-level," recommends drag()/drop(), and its verbose example shows the correct self-gating pattern (cond ? dragProps(...) : {}); (2) the in-file Full API example also passes no options; (3) no real usage (games, MERC, internal) hits this today; (4) impact is bounded — the action controller/engine still validates picks, so a drag on an element invalid for any action gets no drop targets; worst case is a draggable cursor/ghost on "disabled" elements and auto-starting a legal action the UI author intended to gate to another interaction mode. Silent UX-intent override, not correctness/state corruption. Trivial fix: have dragProps evaluate when (or drop `when` into a drag()-only options type so the low-level signature cannot express it).

title: setBeforeAutoExecute() silently replaces any previously registered hook
trap: The hook is single-slot by design ('REPLACES, not accumulated' — but that note is only in the JSDoc). The documented use is animation position capture (`actionController.setBeforeAutoExecute(onBeforeAutoExecute)` from a board component — cribbage does exactly this at CribbageBoard.vue:539). The moment a second component also needs pre-execute capture (e.g. a player-stats panel using the new actionable #player-stats slot props alongside the board), the later registration silently discards the earlier one and the first component's animations start missing their start positions — a very hard-to-attribute breakage since both registrations individually look correct.
rightWay: Coordinating all pre-execute work through one component-owned hook that fans out manually — nothing enforces or even warns about the single-slot constraint at runtime.
suggestion: Either accumulate hooks (run all registered hooks in registration order — the natural expectation) or devWarn on replacement: 'setBeforeAutoExecute called while a hook was already registered; the previous hook has been discarded.'

verdict.reasoning: Verified: setBeforeAutoExecute (useActionController.ts:941) silently overwrites the previous hook; single-slot semantics are intentional (tested at useActionController.test.ts:521) but guarded only by a JSDoc note — no runtime warning, no lint rule, nothing in docs/. The documented pattern (useActionAnimations.ts:28-68) tells every component needing animation capture to call it, and GameShell exposes actionController through multiple slots (game-board and the newly actionable #player-stats slot), so two independently-correct registrations silently clobbering each other is a realistic easy-path failure with a hard-to-attribute symptom (animations lose start positions, no error). Violates the project's own 'fail fast and loud' principle; trivially fixable with a dev-mode warning or hook accumulation. Low severity stands: all current games (cribbage, demo-animation) register exactly once from the board, so no one has hit it yet.

title: boardsmith dev binds 0.0.0.0 by default while its own --host help text implies localhost is the default
trap: A dev runs `boardsmith dev` at a coffee shop or office believing the server is local-only, because the CLI help (src/cli/cli.ts:35) reads "--host <host>  Host to bind the server to (e.g., 0.0.0.0 for network access)" — phrasing that unambiguously implies network access is opt-in. In reality dev.ts:282 defaults `host` to '0.0.0.0', and dev.ts:486 sets Vite `fs.allow` to [uiPath, cwd, boardsmithRoot], so any device on the LAN can read the entire game project AND the whole BoardSmith checkout via Vite's /@fs/ URLs, plus join/act in the running game via the unauthenticated /__boardsmith/ws WebSocket (any 'hello' with any clientId is accepted, multiplayer-host.ts:154).
rightWay: To get a local-only server you must know to pass `--host 127.0.0.1` — but nothing tells you to, and the help text actively teaches the opposite (that omitting --host is the safe choice). Vite itself defaults to localhost precisely because of this risk; BoardSmith silently inverts that default.
suggestion: Default to localhost and make LAN play explicit: `boardsmith dev --lan` (or `--host 0.0.0.0`). If the LAN-by-default product decision stands, fix the --host help text to say the default is 0.0.0.0 and print a loud startup line ("Serving to your whole network — pass --host 127.0.0.1 for local-only"). Either way the help string and the actual default must agree.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual core is confirmed: src/cli/commands/dev.ts:282 defaults host to '0.0.0.0' (deliberately, per the comment "Default to all interfaces so other computers on the LAN can join the game"), while the help text at src/cli/cli.ts:35 ("--host <host>  Host to bind the server to (e.g., 0.0.0.0 for network access)") reads as if network access were opt-in. That mismatch is a genuine documentation/design inconsistency — the help actively teaches the wrong mental model, and it silently inverts Vite's well-known localhost default. No doc in docs/ and no eslint rule addresses it; there is no --host 127.0.0.1 guidance anywhere.

However, the claimed trap ("dev believes the server is local-only") is substantially mitigated by what the CLI actually prints at startup (dev.ts:594-599): for every resolved network URL it prints "Network (others can join): http://x.x.x.x:PORT" in cyan, followed by "Multiplayer: each browser is a player; open the page on another computer to join." The exposure is disclosed loudly on every run — a reasonable developer taking the easy path sees this banner, not the --help text. LAN join is also the core intended feature of the dev host (the whole multiplayer-dev design documented in CLAUDE.md), not an accident. The severity-inflating details also weaken on inspection: the /@fs read exposure is just what any network-bound dev server does with its own project, Vite's default fs.deny still blocks .env/.env.*/certs even inside fs.allow dirs, and the unauthenticated WS join is the product's purpose. So: real (the help text is factually misleading and the safe-default inversion deserves an explicit note or a --host default shown in help), but the fix is a one-line help-text/default-disclosure change, not a high-severity security trap. Severity adjusted from high to low.

title: boardsmith init -t/--template is accepted, documented with a default, and completely ignored
trap: cli.ts:27 registers `-t, --template <template>  Template to use (default: card-game)`, which tells a reasonable dev that other templates exist. Running `boardsmith init my-game -t hex-grid` (or dice-game, etc.) succeeds with "Created my-game successfully!" — but initCommand's `options.template` (declared in InitOptions at init.ts:15-17) is never read anywhere in the function; every invocation scaffolds the identical card game. The dev then spends time deleting deck/hand/card scaffolding they explicitly asked not to get, or worse, assumes hex-grid support is broken.
rightWay: There is only one template. The right way is to not pass -t at all — but the option's existence and its "default: card-game" help text are the documentation, and they lie.
suggestion: Delete the --template option until multiple templates exist, or make init error on any value other than 'card-game' ("Unknown template 'hex-grid'. Available: card-game"). A CLI flag that parses successfully and does nothing is the canonical silent no-op.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: cli.ts:27 registers `-t, --template` with default 'card-game' and multi-template-implying help text, but initCommand (src/cli/commands/init.ts) never reads options.template — the field in InitOptions:16 is dead, and scaffolding is hardcoded to the card game (categories: ['card-game'], card/deck/hand generators). No validation or warning exists for unknown template names, no docs list valid templates, and no lint/type rule catches CLI flag plumbing. Grep confirms no other init template exists anywhere. Worse for the trap: the slash-command aspects directory contains hex-grid.md, dice.md, square-grid.md — exactly the names a dev would plausibly pass to -t and get silent wrong output. This violates the project's own 'fail fast and loud' rule, so it is real. Severity downgraded to low: it is a one-time scaffold command, the card-game output is immediately obvious, nothing is corrupted, and the fix is trivial (remove the option or validate-and-error).

title: --players is silently clamped (and NaN silently produces a zero-seat host); --ai is validated against the pre-clamp count
trap: `boardsmith dev --players 6` on a max-4 game prints no warning: dev.ts:392 clamps to 4 and the dev spends time wondering where seats 5-6 went. `--players 6 --ai 5` is worse: the --ai validation at dev.ts:301 checks against the raw pre-clamp count (6), so seat 5 passes validation, then the clamp makes it nonexistent — the flag is accepted and silently does nothing. And `--players two` (or any typo) parses to NaN, sails through every check (NaN comparisons are all false), and MultiplayerHost's constructor loop `for (seat = 1; seat <= NaN)` (multiplayer-host.ts:141) creates zero seats — the browser opens to a broken empty lobby with no error anywhere.
rightWay: The correct invocation requires already knowing the game's min/max from its gameDefinition; the CLI knows those numbers at the moment it clamps and could simply say so.
suggestion: Fail fast on non-numeric --players/--port/--ai values, and replace the silent clamp with either an error ("--players 6 exceeds this game's max of 4") or at minimum a yellow warning. Validate --ai seats against the effective (post-clamp) player count.

verdict.reasoning: Verified in code: dev.ts:280 parseInt with no NaN check; dev.ts:392 silently clamps (Math.min/max propagate NaN); multiplayer-host.ts:141 loop creates zero seats for NaN so `--players two` starts a broken zero-seat host with no error; dev.ts:301 validates --ai against the pre-clamp count because min/max load later. No type, lint rule, or doc guards this, and the same file loudly validates --port and --ai — --players is the one unvalidated flag, violating the project's own fail-fast rule. However, severity is overstated: line 600 prints `Seats: ${effectivePlayerCount}`, so a 6→4 clamp is visible (Seats: 4) and NaN shows as 'Seats: NaN'; and the vanished --ai pre-mark is nearly moot since open seats play as AI anyway in the dev host. Real pit-of-success gap in dev tooling with trivial recovery → low.

title: Canonical WebSocketMessage union omits UpdateSlotPlayerOptionsMessage, contradicting its own 'invalid messages are unrepresentable' claim
trap: protocol.ts declares itself the single source of truth and the doc block at lines 293-300 promises the discriminated union makes invalid messages unrepresentable. `UpdateSlotPlayerOptionsMessage` is defined at line 401 but omitted from the `WebSocketMessage` union (lines 420-435), which includes its two siblings `UpdatePlayerOptionsMessage` and `UpdateGameOptionsMessage`. A platform implementer writing an exhaustive `switch (message.type)` over `WebSocketMessage` (the advertised pattern) gets no case for the host assigning a slot's options — TypeScript exhaustiveness checking actively confirms their handler is 'complete' while the feature (used by GameShell.vue:1613 for host-assigned exclusive options) is silently unhandled over WS. Conversely, trying to `send()` that message where `WebSocketMessage` is the parameter type is a compile error, pushing devs to cast.
rightWay: Notice the orphaned interface and add it to the union yourself — nothing flags the omission; the type compiles fine and every documented sibling works.
suggestion: Add `UpdateSlotPlayerOptionsMessage` to the `WebSocketMessage` union (or delete the interface if the operation is intentionally HTTP-only, and say so in its doc comment so the union's completeness claim stays true).

verdict.reasoning: The omission is real and provably accidental, not intentional design. Facts verified: (1) `UpdateSlotPlayerOptionsMessage` is defined at src/types/protocol.ts:401 with a `type: 'updateSlotPlayerOptions'` literal but is absent from the `WebSocketMessage` union (lines 420-435), while its siblings `UpdatePlayerOptionsMessage` and `UpdateGameOptionsMessage` are included. (2) Git history refutes any 'intentional omission' defense: the pre-refactor type (ca7f295^, src/session/types.ts:534) DID include 'updateSlotPlayerOptions' in the type-string union; the audit2-U6 refactor (ca7f295) that converted it to a discriminated union created the interface but dropped it from the union — a silent regression in the very commit whose purpose was 'single-source' protocol types. (3) No lint rule or type check flags an orphaned interface, and the doc block (lines 293-300) explicitly promises completeness, so nothing guards the trap. However, the practical blast radius is much smaller than 'medium' implies: I found zero in-repo consumers that dispatch on WebSocketMessage — the shipped client (src/client/game-connection.ts, client/types.ts:238) only ever sends 'action' | 'ping' | 'getState' over WS, and ALL lobby operations including updateSlotPlayerOptions go over HTTP POST (src/client/client.ts:492, /games/:id/slot-player-options). GameShell.vue:1613 calls the HTTP client method, so the host-assigned-options feature works regardless of the union. The failure scenario requires an external platform implementer to build a WS-transport lobby server from this union AND a custom client that sends lobby ops over WS — the reference stack never exercises that path. Real defect (public exported protocol type contradicts its own contract, one-line fix), but severity low given no shipped code path is affected.

title: TestGame.doAction never throws, and the flagship doc example models ignoring its result — tests pass while every move silently fails
trap: `doAction` returns an `ActionExecutionResult`; a failed action (wrong seat, unavailable action, bad args) is just `{ success: false }`. The class-level example at test-game.ts:101-102 models the trap verbatim: `testGame.doAction(1, 'ask', { target: 2, rank: 'K' }); expect(testGame.isComplete()).toBe(false);` — that test passes even if 'ask' failed, because a failed action also leaves the game incomplete. Docs repeat the unchecked pattern (docs/api/testing.md:404, docs/agent-control.md:165). A dev writing setup moves (`doAction; doAction; expect(finalState)`) whose first move is rejected gets a green test asserting on a game that never happened, or a confusing failure three moves later with no pointer to the rejected move.
rightWay: Use `assertActionSucceeds()` (simulate-action.ts:113) or `testGame.action(...).execute()` (action-builder.ts:91), both of which throw with actionable messages — but they are secondary, less-discoverable APIs, while `doAction` is the method every example reaches for first.
suggestion: Make `doAction` throw on failure by default (with the rich debugActionAvailability trace assertActionAvailable already builds), and offer `tryAction()` returning the result for tests that expect failure — or at minimum fix the TestGame/doc examples to check `result.success` and steer setup code to assertActionSucceeds.

verdict.reasoning: Partially confirmed. doAction (src/testing/test-game.ts:272) does return ActionExecutionResult without throwing, and the class-level JSDoc example (lines 101-102) models the unchecked pattern with an assertion (isComplete() === false) that passes even when the action fails; docs/api/testing.md:404 and docs/agent-control.md:165 repeat unchecked calls, and real game tests in ~/BoardSmithGames mostly use unchecked doAction (assertActionSucceeds appears once across all games). However, the auditor overstates discoverability: assertActionSucceeds is the FIRST pattern in the testing docs quickstart (docs/api/testing.md:78-92) and in the boardsmith/testing module docstring (src/testing/index.ts:17-23), and doAction's own method-level docstring (test-game.ts:264-270) explicitly models checking result.success. The non-throwing return is also a deliberate design serving the agent/playout use case (enumerateLegalMoves loops in agent-control.md) where failure is a normal outcome. The residual real issue is that the most prominent JSDoc surface (class-level example, IDE hover) models silent-failure, contradicting the project's fail-fast rule — a doc-example fix, not an API flaw. Severity adjusted from medium to low.

title: TestGame's default seed is `test-${Date.now()}` — nondeterministic by default, contradicting the library's own deterministic-by-default doctrine
trap: Omitting `seed` (it's optional) gives every run a wall-clock seed, so any test whose game shuffles or rolls becomes intermittently flaky in CI, and the failing run cannot be reproduced unless the dev knows the seed lives at `testGame.runner.seed` (undocumented on TestGame; it isn't printed on failure). Meanwhile the same module's `playUntilComplete` (simulate-action.ts:313) explicitly documents 'Deterministic by default … NEVER falls back to Math.random', and `simulateRandomGames` surfaces its generated seed on the results for replay — TestGame is the one testing entry point that quietly does the opposite.
rightWay: Always pass `seed:` in TestGameOptions — the docs' examples do, but nothing enforces it and the no-seed call compiles and usually passes, so the omission survives until a shuffle-dependent assertion flakes weeks later.
suggestion: Default to a fixed literal seed (matching playUntilComplete's design), or keep it random but surface it: expose `testGame.seed` and include it in assertion-helper failure messages so any flake is one copy-paste from a deterministic repro.

verdict.reasoning: Confirmed: src/testing/test-game.ts:127 defaults seed to `test-${Date.now()}`, making no-seed TestGame runs nondeterministic. No guardrail exists — seed is optional in TestGameOptions, no eslint rule enforces it, and the CLI scaffold provides no seeded template. The easy path is demonstrably taken: ~34 of ~98 TestGame.create calls in BoardSmith's own test suite omit seed. The generated seed is captured on GameRunner (runner.seed, src/runtime/runner.ts:98-119) but is undocumented on TestGame and never printed on failure, so a flaky CI run is not practically reproducible. Crucially, the same module contradicts itself: playUntilComplete (simulate-action.ts:311-315) explicitly comments 'Deterministic by default' and uses the fixed literal 'playUntilComplete-default', and simulateRandomGames surfaces its seed for replay — so TestGame is the sole testing entry point violating the library's own doctrine, with the correct pattern (fixed literal default) already modeled two files away. Severity stays low: test-tooling flakiness only, seed technically recoverable, and docs examples consistently show passing seed.

title: Error message tells devs to 'Provide an explicit playerId in MeepleClientConfig' — but MeepleClientConfig has no playerId field
trap: In an environment without Web Crypto, `generatePlayerId()` throws: 'Provide an explicit playerId in MeepleClientConfig…'. A dev following that actionable advice writes `new MeepleClient({ baseUrl, playerId })` and gets a TypeScript excess-property error, because `MeepleClientConfig` (src/client/types.ts:12-27) has no such field — the only real escape hatch is the unmentioned `client.setPlayerId()`, which can't be reached since the constructor throws first.
rightWay: Discover `setPlayerId()` by reading the source — impossible anyway, because the exception is thrown from inside the constructor before any instance exists to call it on.
suggestion: Add `playerId?: string` to MeepleClientConfig (it's also what apps persisting identity across sessions want — today they must construct, then setPlayerId, hoping nothing captured the transient generated id), and have the constructor skip generation when provided.

verdict.reasoning: Verified: MeepleClientConfig (src/client/types.ts:12-27) has no playerId field, yet the error at src/client/client.ts:585-589 instructs devs to provide one there; TypeScript's excess-property check rejects that advice. generatePlayerId() is invoked from the constructor (line 37), so setPlayerId() (line 542) — the only real escape hatch — is unreachable and also undocumented (docs/api/client.md never mentions it as client config). No lint rule or doc guardrail mitigates this. The throw path is rare (only environments lacking Web Crypto, i.e. pre-Node-19 or exotic runtimes; the message's own 'Node 16+' claim is also inaccurate since global crypto landed un-flagged in Node 19), which bounds impact, but a dev who does hit it gets actionable-sounding advice that is un-followable — a direct violation of the project's 'error messages should be actionable' rule. Real, severity stays low.
